sentences: Los hutíes de Yemen toman el control de Mocha: ¿qué puede pasar con el estrecho de Bab el-Mandeb?
Auditado por: Comscore Asociado a: IAB Perú Licenciado por: APDAYC Mundo Medio Oriente Los hutíes de Yemen toman el control de Mocha: ¿qué puede pasar con el estrecho de Bab el-Mandeb?

Según confirmaron cuatro fuentes militares del Gobierno de Yemen reconocido internacionalmente a la agencia Reuters, los rebeldes hutíes entraron este 10 de septiembre en la ciudad de Mocha, a unos 80 kilómetros del estrecho de Bab el-Mandeb, luego del repliegue de las fuerzas progubernamentales.

Además, en la provincia de Taiz –a la que pertenece Mocha–, militares yemeníes informaron que los rebeldes se apoderaron de la zona de al-Shaqira, una importante ruta de abastecimiento que conecta la ciudad de Taiz –capital de la provincia homónima– y otras zonas del interior con la costa oeste de Yemen.

| Fuente: EFE | Fotógrafo: YAHYA ARHAB por France 24 Agrega RPP en Actualizado el 10 de Set, 2026 11:40 am Fuentes militares y testigos confirmaron la entrada de los rebeldes respaldados por Irán en la histórica ciudad portuaria de Mocha , en las costas del mar Rojo .
Esto representa el mayor avance del grupo hacia el estrecho de Bab el-Mandeb desde el inicio de la guerra civil en Yemen en 2014.

Yemen parece cada vez más cerca de la reactivación a gran escala de su cruenta guerra civil ante el creciente avance de los rebeldes hutíes respaldados por Irán en la zona costera del occidente del país y los reportes de bombardeos de Arabia Saudita , que lidera la coalición en apoyo a las fuerzas progubernamentales.

Hasta la firma de un frágil cese al fuego en 2022, el conflicto iniciado en 2014 en el país de 40 millones de habitantes se había cobrado la vida de 150 000 personas y había causado una de las crisis humanitarias de mayor magnitud del mundo, con millones de yemeníes viviendo al borde de la hambruna o fuera del alcance de la asistencia .
El progreso de la avanzada militar de los hutíes alcanzó este 10 de septiembre un nuevo hito: la toma del control de la histórica ciudad portuaria de Mocha, en las costas del mar Rojo.

Amin al-Mohammdi, residente de la ciudad portuaria, aseguró que los hutíes han cerrado todas las carreteras de la costa oeste que conducen a Mocha y los comercios de la ciudad han clausurado sus puertas.

Uno de sus líderes militares, Tarek Saleh –sobrino del asesinado presidente yemení Ali Abdullah Saleh – ordenó establecer un centro de comando alternativo en una ubicación segura, según reportó el canal 'Al-Jumhuriya', vinculado a esta figura.

La importancia de Mocha se explica en su ubicación sobre las costas del mar Rojo –que le ha permitido ser un relevante punto de ingreso de comida y otros elementos de la ayuda internacional, ahora en peligro–, su proximidad con Bab el-Mandeb y su valor histórico por haber sido el puerto comercial de café más importante del mundo.

No se trata del único logro reciente de los rebeldes hutíes, que han acelerado su avance en el frente de la costa occidental de Yemen, lo que le puede otorgar una posición ventajosa para perturbar el comercio marítimo .
Unas personas circulan en moto por una calle de Saná, en Yemen, el 5 de septiembre de 2026.

Yemen está viviendo una escalada de los combates en la ciudad de Taiz, al suroeste del país, entre las fuerzas gubernamentales respaldadas por Arabia Saudí y los combatientes hutíes, lo que ha provocado el desplazamiento de casi 1.800 familias en los últimos dos días, según un comunicado de la Oficina de Coordinación de Asuntos Humanitarios de la ONU (OCHA).
Los rebeldes hutíes también han lanzado ataques contra las estratégicas islas Hanish, situadas frente a las costas de Mocha.

Una captura de pantalla extraída de un vídeo sin fecha publicado el 9 de septiembre de 2026 y facilitado por el centro de comunicación militar hutí muestra a combatientes hutíes inspeccionando un vehículo blindado dañado de las fuerzas gubernamentales durante los combates en la provincia de Al-Jawf, al oeste de Yemen.

| Fuente: EFE | Fotógrafo: HOUTHI MILITARY MEDIA CENTER HANDOUT También es vital para el tráfico procedente del oleoducto Suez-Mediterráneo, situado en la costa egipcia del mar Rojo, y para las mercancías con destino a Asia, incluido el petróleo ruso.

Bab el-Mandeb se ubica en el extremo meridional del mar Rojo, entre Yemen, en la Península Arábiga, y Yibuti y Eritrea, en la costa africana, además de estar al lado opuesto de la península con respecto al estrecho de Ormuz, que ha estado en el centro del conflicto entre Estados Unidos e Irán.
Combatientes hutíes desfilan durante una campaña para movilizar a más combatientes en medio de una escalada de los combates, en Saná (Yemen), el 10 de septiembre de 2026.

Las operaciones militares entre los hutíes y las fuerzas gubernamentales respaldadas por Arabia Saudí se han intensificado en todo Yemen, lo que ha provocado que los enfrentamientos se extiendan a varias ciudades.

Desde hace algunas semanas, el frágil cese al fuego en Yemen ha sido puesto a prueba por este avance de los hutíes en la costa occidental del país y sus recientes ataques a sitios civiles y económicos de Arabia Saudita, que han causado más de 70 heridos.

Riad –que desde 2015 lidera la coalición progubernamental frente a los hutíes, como una forma de contrarrestar la influencia iraní en la región– ha atacado semanas atrás el aeropuerto internacional de Saná y en los últimos días, las fuerzas leales al Ejecutivo yemení han intensificado sus ataques aéreos contra posiciones rebeldes.
Asimismo, de acuerdo con la misma agencia de noticias, varios comandantes del Cuerpo de la Guardia Revolucionaria Islámica viajaron a Yemen para ayudar a coordinar esas acciones.

tool.excerpt: The East–West Pipeline, also known as the Petroline, is a 1,201-kilometre-long (746 mi) pipeline in Saudi Arabia that runs from the Abqaiq oil field in the Eastern Province (near Bahrain and Qatar on the Persian Gulf coast) across the width of the Arabian Peninsula, to Yanbu at the Red Sea. It was built during the Iran–Iraq War in the 1980s to allow Saudi oil exports to bypass the tanker war taking place in the Strait of Hormuz. == Pipeline description == The pipeline has two pipes, one 142 centimetres (56 in) in diameter and the other, originally for natural gas liquids, 122 centimetres (48 in) in diameter. In 2018, they had a capacity of 5 million barrels per day (790,000 m3/d) (BPD) during normal operation. In 2026, its full capacity was 7 million BPD when accompanying natural gas liquids pipelines were converted to carry crude oil. Saudi Aramco's East-West Pipeline links oil production facilities in the Eastern Province with Yanbu on the west coast, providing export flexibility between the kingdom's east and west coasts. Typically, the pipeline supplies oil to a number of locations: 1 million BPD to 3 refineries in Yanbu (controlled by the Yanbu National Petrochemical Company and Aramco), to the Sumed pipeline in Egypt, and 1.1–1.4 million BPD of Arab Light oil through the King Fahd Industrial Port (Yanbu) with a limit of 3 million BPD. Yanbu port's two terminals, Yanbu North and Yanbu South, have a nominal loading capacity of about 4.5 million BPD, but a tested actual capacity of about 4 million BPD. tool.title: East–West Crude Oil Pipeline
tool.excerpt: The East–West Pipeline, also known as the Petroline, is a 1,201-kilometre-long (746 mi) pipeline in Saudi Arabia that runs from the Abqaiq oil field in the Eastern Province (near Bahrain and Qatar on the Persian Gulf coast) across the width of the Arabian Peninsula, to Yanbu at the Red Sea. It was built during the Iran–Iraq War in the 1980s to allow Saudi oil exports to bypass the tanker war taking place in the Strait of Hormuz. == Pipeline description == The pipeline has two pipes, one 142 centimetres (56 in) in diameter and the other, originally for natural gas liquids, 122 centimetres (48 in) in diameter. In 2018, they had a capacity of 5 million barrels per day (790,000 m3/d) (BPD) during normal operation. In 2026, its full capacity was 7 million BPD when accompanying natural gas liquids pipelines were converted to carry crude oil. Saudi Aramco's East-West Pipeline links oil production facilities in the Eastern Province with Yanbu on the west coast, providing export flexibility between the kingdom's east and west coasts. Typically, the pipeline supplies oil to a number of locations: 1 million BPD to 3 refineries in Yanbu (controlled by the Yanbu National Petrochemical Company and Aramco), to the Sumed pipeline in Egypt, and 1.1–1.4 million BPD of Arab Light oil through the King Fahd Industrial Port (Yanbu) with a limit of 3 million BPD. Yanbu port's two terminals, Yanbu North and Yanbu South, have a nominal loading capacity of about 4.5 million BPD, but a tested actual capacity of about 4 million BPD. In 2026, consultancy Vortexa estimated that in wartime conditions, capacity would be about 3 million BPD. == History == The pipeline was built in the 1980s, "amid fears that the Iran-Iraq war would cut off shipping through the Strait of Hormuz." The pipeline has been converted at times to carry natural gas, and later converted back to carry crude oil. The 2019 Afif attack by Houthi drones targeted the pipeline in May 2019, temporarily shutting it down. During the 2026 Iran war and the closure of the Strait of Hormuz to non-Iranian vessels, it was converted to full capacity on 11 March 2026. tool.excerpt: === Delayed production start === The original concession of 14 March 1925 covered all of Iraq, but IPC was reluctant to develop it quickly and production was restricted to fields constituting only one-half of 1 percent of the country's total area. During the Great Depression, the world was awash with oil and greater output from Iraq would simply have driven the price down to even lower levels. Delaying tactics were employed not only in actual drilling and development, but also in conducting negotiations on such matters as pipeline rights-of-way. The owners of IPC had conflicting interests: the Anglo-Persian Oil Company, Royal Dutch/Shell and Standard Oil had access to major sources of crude oil outside Iraq, and therefore wanted to hold the Iraqi concessions in reserve, whilst CFP and the other companies pushed for rapid development of Iraqi oil as they had limited crude oil supplies. These competing interests delayed the development of the Iraqi fields, and IPC's concession eventually expired because the companies failed to meet certain performance requirements, such as the construction of pipelines and shipping terminals. ... tool.excerpt: At its narrowest point, the Strait is 21 miles wide, but the width of the shipping lane in either direction is only two miles, separated by a two-mile buffer zone. The Strait is deep and wide enough to handle the world's largest crude oil tankers, with about two-thirds of oil shipments carried by tankers in excess of 150,000 deadweight tons. Several alternatives are potentially available to move oil from the Persian Gulf region without transiting Hormuz, but they are limited in capacity, in many cases are not currently operating or operable, and generally engender higher transport costs and logistical challenges. Alternate routes include the 745-mile Petroline, also known as the East-West Pipeline, across Saudi Arabia from Abqaiq to the Red Sea. The East-West Pipeline has a nameplate capacity of about 5 million bbl/d, with current movements estimated at about 2 million bbl/d. ... sentences: Alternate routes include the 745-mile Petroline, also known as the East-West Pipeline, across Saudi Arabia from Abqaiq to the Red Sea.
The East-West Pipeline has a nameplate capacity of about 5 million bbl/d, with current movements estimated at about 2 million bbl/d.
Other alternate routes could include the deactivated 1.65-million bbl/d Iraqi Pipeline across Saudi Arabia (IPSA) and the deactivated 0.5 million-bbl/d Tapline to Lebanon.
Government, Selected Oil and Gas Pipeline Infrastructure in the Middle East .
The Strait of Hormuz (shown in the oval on the map), which is located between Oman and Iran , connects the Persian Gulf with the Gulf of Oman and the Arabian Sea.
The Abqaiq-Yanbu natural gas liquids pipeline, which runs parallel to the Petroline to the Red Sea, has a 290,000-bbl/d capacity.

Additional oil could also be pumped north via the Iraq-Turkey pipeline to the port of Ceyhan on the Mediterranean Sea, but volumes have been limited by the closure of the Strategic Pipeline linking north and south Iraq.
The United Arab Emirates is also completing the 1.5 million bbl/d Abu Dhabi Crude Oil Pipeline that will cross the emirate of Abu Dhabi and end at the port of Fujairah just south of the Strait.

EIA's World Oil Transit Chokepoints analysis brief contains additional information about other chokepoints, and the Middle East & North Africa overview contains additional information about countries in the region.

tool.title: Economic impact of the 2026 Iran war
tool.excerpt: The conflict coincided with historically low European gas storage levels—estimated at just 30% capacity following a harsh 2025–2026 winter—causing Dutch TTF gas benchmarks to nearly double to over €60/MWh by mid-March. Consequently, the European Central Bank (ECB) postponed its planned interest rate reductions on 19 March, raising its 2026 inflation forecast and cutting GDP growth projections, with economists warning that energy-intensive economies face high risks of technical recession if the maritime blockade persists through the summer refill season. The crisis has further impacted industrial output in the United Kingdom and the EU, where chemical and steel manufacturers have imposed surcharges of up to 30% to offset surging electricity and feedstock costs, potentially leading to permanent deindustrialization in some sectors. The economic impact on Europe has been characterized by a severe energy-supply shock and industrial strain, with the European Central Bank (ECB) warning that a prolonged conflict will likely trigger a period of stagflation, a period of low growth rates accompanied by inflation, and push major energy-dependent economies, including Germany and Italy, into technical recession by the end of 2026. British company Shell had issued a warning that Europe could face a shortage of fuel as early as April. ... The 2026 Iran war, including the closure of the Strait of Hormuz, has led to what the International Energy Agency has characterized as the "largest supply disruption in the history of the global oil market". The conflict has echoed the 1970s energy crisis through acute supply shortages, currency volatility, inflation and heightened risks of stagflation and recession. A 2026 market analysis by MCB Group placed the current disruption alongside four earlier oil-market shocks, noting that in each case the initial price spike proved larger than the eventual sustained increase.
